rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted exchange is compressed for brevity, implying Moses and Aaron promptly obeyed and their words to Pharaoh needed no explicit retelling.
rows.anchor: بعد ما اتياه وبلغاه ما امرا به وإنما طوى ذكر ذلك للايجاز والأشعار بأنهما كما امرا بذلك سارعا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the brothers waited at Pharaoh’s gate for a time before admission, then entered after a severe screen was lifted.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنهما لما أمر اباتيانه وقول ما ذكر له جاءا جميعا إلى بابه فاقاما حينا لا يؤذن لهما

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb reports Moses’ fearless entry among trained lions, the staff becoming a serpent and killing many, Pharaoh’s request for a forty-day delay, and the lions escorting Moses out.
rows.anchor: عن وهب بن منبه أن الله تعالى لما أمر موسى عليه السلام بما أمر أقبل إلى فرعون في مدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron was apparently with Moses at the encounter; the Wahb report may omit him because it focuses on Moses.
rows.anchor: واظاهر أن هرون كان معه حين الآيتان ولعله إنما لم يذكر في هذا الخبر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One report says Asiya urged acceptance of the brothers’ call, while Haman opposed it as a loss of mastery and lordship.
rows.anchor: شاور آسية فقالت ما ينبغي لأحد أن يرد ما دعيا إليه فشاور هامان وكان لا يبت أمرا دون رايه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For such stories, rely on revelation and disregard other accounts unless their soundness is established.
rows.anchor: والأولى في أمثال هذه القصص الاكتفاء بما في المنزل وعدم الالتفات إلى غيره إلا أن يوثق بصحته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Wahb account’s forty-day reprieve conflicts with Moses later setting the festival day as the appointment; the encounter apparently did not happen twice.
rows.anchor: فإن كون فرعون جعل الأجل يعكر عليه ما سيأتي إن شاء الله تعالى من قول موسى عليه السلام حين طلب منه فرعون أن يجعل موعدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is an explanatory resumption: the text supplies what Pharaoh said after the brothers delivered their message.
rows.anchor: والجملة استئناف بياني كأنه قيل فماذا قال حين أتياه وقالا له ما قالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh does not call God his own Lord, even while quoting the brothers’ words, because of his extreme arrogance and tyranny.
rows.anchor: لغاية عتوه ونهاية طغيانه بل اضافه اليهما لما أن المرسل لابد أن يكون ربا للرسول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the brothers had already declared God Lord of all, while naming Pharaoh’s lordship alone sufficed for the immediate point.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لأنهما قد صرحا بربوبيته تعالى للكل بأن قالا : انا رسول رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed fa makes Pharaoh’s question follow from the brothers’ claim to be messengers of their Lord: he asks who sent them.
rows.anchor: والفاء لترتيب السؤال على ما سبق من كونهما رسولي ربهما أي إذا كنتما رسولي ربكما الذي ارسلكما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh addresses Moses alone because he recognizes him as the principal messenger and Aaron as his minister.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص النداء بموسى عليه السلام مع توجيه الخطاب اليهما لما ظهر له من أنه الأصل في الرسالة وهرون وزيره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further possibility is that Pharaoh taunts Moses as his own dependent, recalling that he raised him as a child.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون للتعريض بأنه ربه كما قال : الم نربك فينا وليدا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some exegetes say Pharaoh knew Moses had a speech impediment and wanted to silence him; this assumes the impediment persisted to some degree.
rows.anchor: لأنه قد عرف أن له عليه السلام رتة فاراد أن يسكتة وهو مبنى على ما عليه كثير من المفسرين من بقاء رتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses gives the answer because Pharaoh directed the question to him in particular.
rows.anchor: أي موسى عليه السلام واستبد بالجواب من حيث أنه خص بالسؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, “our Lord” is the subject and the relative clause its predicate; alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted “He is,” with the relative as modifier.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هو ربنا والموصول صفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person plural may mean Moses and Aaron, or, as some investigators argue, all creatures, answering Pharaoh by establishing the truth.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المحققين : اراد جميع المخلوقات تحقيقا للحق وردا عن اللعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the first parsing, “everything” is the first object and “its creation” the second; the latter is a passive participle, and its pronoun refers to “everything.”
rows.anchor: مفعول أول لاعطى و ( خلقه ) مفعوله الثانى وهو مصدر بمعنى اسم المفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universal applies to individuals: God gives each its dispositionally sought or fitting form, shape, benefit, and properties, as the eye and ear suit seeing and hearing.
rows.anchor: أي أعطى كل شئ من الأشياء الأمر الذي طلبه بلسان استعداده من الصورة والشكل والمنفعة والمضرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed reading keeps “creation” as a verbal noun, meaning each thing receives the act of creating suited to its readiness or proper form; al-Alusi considers it weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الخلق باق على مصدريته بمعنى الايجاد أي أعطى كل شئ الايجاد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict “everything” to kinds rather than individuals, to avoid incomplete individuals caused by incidental defects.
rows.anchor: وحمل بعضهم العموم على عموم الأنواع دون عموم الأفراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects narrowing the scope: Sunni consensus holds God creates and commands through wisdom as grace, not obligation; each thing is complete in its rank, and creation shows no disparity.
rows.anchor: والحق أن الله تعالى راعى الحكمة فيما خلق وأمر تفضلا ورحمة لاوجوبا وهذا مما اجمع عليه أهل السنة والجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past tense is no reason to restrict the scope to kinds: although many individuals are yet to exist, kinds already exist and no new kind need arise; the proposed objection remains debatable.
rows.anchor: سبب العدول كون ( أعطى ) حقيقة فى الماضى فلو حمل كل شئ على عموم الأفراد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن جبير، السدي
rows.claim: They explain the phrase as each animal being given a female counterpart resembling it in form, treating “all” as indicating abundance.
rows.anchor: وروى عن ابن عباس وابن جبير والسدى أن المعنى أعطى كل حيوان ذكر نظيره فى الخلق والصورة انثى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi treats the animal-pairing interpretation as an example of the broader fitting-gift meaning, not a literal universal, and doubts that its named authorities intended the literal claim.
rows.anchor: وعندى أن هذا المعنى من فروع المعنى السابق الذى ذكرناه ولعل مراد من قاله التمثيل وإلا فهو بعيد جدا

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba’i reverses the objects: “its creation” is first, while “everything” is second, meaning God gives creatures what they need; al-Alusi finds the usual parsing clearer in wording and meaning.
rows.anchor: ونسب هذا القول إلى الجبائى والأول اظهر لفظا ومعنى

rows.speaker: عبد الله، وأناس من أصحاب رسول الله، وأبو نهيك، وابن أبي إسحاق، والأعمش، والحسن، ونصير، وابن نوح، وسلام
rows.claim: These authorities read “creation” as the active past verb “he created”; the clause modifies the preceding noun, with the second object elided as context supplies it.
rows.anchor: وقرا عبد الله واناس من اصحاب رسول الله ( صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, God gave each created thing what repairs or benefits it, or what it needs.
rows.anchor: أي أعطى كل شئ خلقه تعالى ما يصلحه أو ما يحتاج اليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari likens the construction to “gives and withholds”: God has not left any created thing without gift and favor; al-Kashf calls this clearer and more eloquent, while al-Alusi remains hesitant.
rows.anchor: وجعل ذلك الزمخشرى من باب يعطى ويمنع أي كل شئ خلقه سبحانه لم يخله من عطائه وانعامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi considers the other grammatical analysis better crafted and more fitting to context, and closer to the first reading’s initial interpretation.
rows.anchor: الأول احسن صناعة وموافقه المقام وهو عندى أوفق بالمعنى الأول للقراءة الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then he guided” means God directed and showed the way; these created things point to their maker, whose existence, wisdom, and generosity they demonstrate.
rows.anchor: أي ارشد ودل سبحانه بذلك على وجوده وجوده فان من نظر في هذه المحدثات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then” marks rank, not elapsed time: guidance follows creation in ontological order, though no time separates them.
rows.anchor: وهذا الجعل وان كان متأخر بالذات عن الخلق وليس بينهما تراخ في الزمان اصلا

rows.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: Al-Irshad explains guidance as teaching each creature how to benefit from its gifts and attain preservation and perfection, by choice in animals and natural powers in other beings.
rows.anchor: طريق الانتفاع والارتفاق بما اعطاه وعرفه كيف يتوصل إلى بقائه وكماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi objects that creation is linguistically broader than bodily assembly and already includes moving and perceiving powers; this interpretation also makes “guided” metaphorical.
rows.anchor: الخلق لغة اعم مما ذكره وان القوى المحركة والمدركة داخلة فى عموم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومن معه
rows.claim: A transmitted interpretation says God guided creatures to union through affinity and mating; other interpretations are also mentioned without detail.
rows.anchor: على التفسير المروى عن ابن عباس ومن معه ثم هداه إلى الاجتماع بالفة والمناكحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi praises the answer as concise, comprehensive, and clear to a fair seeker; instead of the obvious title “Lord of the worlds,” Moses points to the origination, dependence, and differing ranks of all beings.
rows.anchor: سلك طريق الارشاد والاسلوب الحكيم واشار إلى حدوث الموجودات باسرها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer Pharaoh knew God but rebelled: the relative clause had to be known to him, and its claim about creation would identify its Lord.
rows.anchor: استدل بالاية على أن فرعون كان عارفا بالله تعالى إلا أنه كان معاندا لأن جملة الصلة لا بد أن تكون معلومة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The argument also cites Pharaoh’s acknowledgment that Moses’ signs came from the Lord of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: لقد علمت ما انزل هؤلاء إلا رب السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: They cite the statement that the opponents inwardly knew the signs were true but denied them unjustly and arrogantly.
rows.anchor: وجحدوا بها واستيقنتها أنفسهم ظلما وعلوا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: They cite the account that Pharaoh and his people thought they would not return to God, construing this as denial of resurrection rather than of the Creator.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى في سورة القصص : ( وظنوا أنهم الينا لا يرجعون ) فانه ليس فيه إلا انكار المعاد دون المبدا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: They read Pharaoh’s “Who is the Lord of the worlds?” as asking for God’s essence, while his description of Moses’ Lord as a madman implies acknowledgment of existence.
rows.anchor: ان رسولكم الذى ارسل اليكم لمجنون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: They argue Pharaoh was rational and so knew he arose after nonexistence and needed a governor; his limited realm also undercuts belief that he created the whole world.
rows.anchor: وكل عاقل يعلم بالضرورة أنه وجد بعد العدم ومن كان كذلك افتقر إلى مدبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the question “who?” apparently followed a proof of existence; Moses then moved to the harder issue of divine essence, which humans cannot know, though these arguments are disputable.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن السؤال بمن سابق فكان موسى عليه السلام لما أقام الدلالة على الوجود ترك المنازعة معه في هذا المقام

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: Others hold Pharaoh ignorant of God; proposed forms include denying any maker, necessary-cause philosophy, star or idol worship, indwelling, and anthropomorphism.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من قال : أنه كان جاهلا بالله تعالى بعد اتفاقهم على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s claim to be lord over his subjects means they must obey him and not devote themselves to another’s command.
rows.anchor: وأما ادعاؤه الربوبية لنفسه فبمعنى أنه يجب على من تحت يده طاعته والانقياد له وعدم الاشتغال بطاعة غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even Pharaoh began an argument and requested proof rather than resorting to abuse; sophistry against a caller to truth is disgraceful, and Muslims should not approve what Pharaoh avoided.
rows.anchor: واستدل فى شروعه فى المناظرة وطلب الحجة دون السفاهة والشغب مع كونه جبارا شديد البطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ proof exposes blind imitation and the error of claiming that knowledge of God comes from a messenger’s assertion; one may quote an opponent with the reply and must hear the objection to answer it.
rows.anchor: على فساد التقليد فى امثال هذا المطلوب وفساد قول القائل : أن معرفة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing Moses’ brilliant proof, Pharaoh feared that its truth and the falsity of his own claims would become plain, so he tried to divert Moses to irrelevant history and make him appear uninformed.
rows.anchor: لما شاهد اللعين ما نظمه عليه السلام فى سلك الجواب من البرهان النير على الطراز الرائع خاف أن يظهر للناس حقية مقالاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “bal” first means thought, as in something crossing one’s mind, then denotes a noteworthy state or concern; its plural is not normally used.
rows.anchor: وهو المراد ولا يثنى ولا يجمع إلا شذوذا فى قولهم بالات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fa links the question to the messenger claim: if Moses is a messenger, Pharaoh asks him to report what happened to earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: وكان الفاء لتفريع ما بعدها على دعوى الرسالة أي إذا كنت رسولا فاخبرنى ما حال القرون الماضية والأمم الخالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers that the generations’ detailed histories are unseen matters known only to God; he is a servant who knows only what revelation gives him for his mission.
rows.anchor: أي أن ذلك من الغيوب التى لا يعلمها إلا الله تعالى وإنما أنا عبد لا أعلم منها إلا ما علمنيه من الأمور المتعلقة بالرسالة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view is that Pharaoh asked to test whether Moses was a prophet or merely a storyteller familiar with old nations.
rows.anchor: سأله عن ذلك ليختبر أنه نبى أو هو من جملة القصاص الذين دارسوا قصص الأمم

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says Pharaoh asked after hearing the believer from Pharaoh’s family warn his people of the day of the confederates; Moses returned the knowledge to God because the Torah had not yet been revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش : أن اللعين لما سمع وعظ مؤمن آل فرعون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view links the question to “peace on whoever follows guidance”: Pharaoh asks about the dead generations’ happiness or misery, and Moses says God knows the detail.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : أن السؤال مبنى على قوله عليه السلام ( والسلام على من اتبع الهدى )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the preceding general statement already answers that interpretation: whoever follows guidance is safe, while whoever turns away is punished.
rows.anchor: فاندفع ما قيل : أنه لو كان المؤول عنه ما ذكر من السعادة والشقاوة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another proposal links the question to the revelation claim: why did earlier generations deny it and then suffer punishment?
rows.anchor: إذا كان الأمر كذلك فما بال القرون الأولى كذبوا ثم ما عذبوا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view takes the question to concern resurrection and the pronoun in “their knowledge” to refer to the Day of Judgment; al-Alusi dismisses these proposals and especially the pronoun’s reference to resurrection.
rows.anchor: هو متعلق به والسؤال عن البعث والضمير فى ( علمها ) للقيامة وكلا القولين كما ترى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation makes Pharaoh challenge how God could encompass the details of numerous, ancient peoples; Moses replies that divine knowledge includes them all.
rows.anchor: اعتراضا على ما تضمنه من علمه تعالى بتفاصيل الأشياء وجزئياتها المستتبع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The generations are singled out because Pharaoh knew some of them and could test Moses’ truth, or because he wanted to trap Moses quickly before a broad answer prolonged matters.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص القرون الأولى على هذا بالذكر مع أولوية التعميم قيل لعلم فرعون ببعضها وبذلك يتمكن من معرفة صدق موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi calls this interpretation remote and rejects the objection that naming earlier peoples weakens it, since naming all things would make the trap clearer and stronger.
rows.anchor: فانه لو اخذها بجملتها كان أظهر وأقوى في تمشى ما اراد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another challenge asks why earlier peoples failed to infer the Creator from such a clear proof; a related view asks why they did not infer from God’s guidance, with both answers referring to divine decree.
rows.anchor: ما بال القرون الأولى نسوه سبحانه ولم يؤمنوا به تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a book” is parsed with “with my Lord” as the first predicate and “in a book” as the second; Abu al-Baqa lists alternatives, but a verbal noun cannot govern beyond its predicate.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه خبر ثان لعلمها والخبر الأول عند ربى وجوز أن يكونا خبرا واحدا مثل هذا حلو حامض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers “with my Lord” as the first predicate and “in a book” as the second; the book may be the Preserved Tablet, with its actual inscriptions standing for the recorded knowledge.
rows.anchor: وانت تعلم أن أول الأوجه هو الأوجه وكأنه عنى عليه السلام بالكتاب اللوح المحفوظ أي علمها مثبت في اللوح المحفوظ بتفاصيله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “book” can mean an ordinary register, a simile for how firmly the knowledge is established in God’s knowledge; al-Alusi considers this perhaps preferable, as the next clause suggests.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون المراد بالكتاب الدفتر كما هو المعروف فى اللغة ويكون ذلك تمثيلا لتمكنه وتقرره فى علمه عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On either reading, “He neither errs nor forgets” prevents the thought that God records matters because he fears forgetting; the Tablet’s record instead serves divine purposes.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن فيه على الوجهين دفع توهم الاحتياج لأن الأثبات في الكتاب إنما يفعله من يفعله لخوف النسيان

rows.speaker: القفال وبعض المحققين
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal and some investigators take “does not err” as never omitting anything from divine knowledge and “does not forget” as never losing what is already known; al-Alusi approves this reading.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الجملتين بما ذكر مما ذهب اليه القفال ووافقه بعض المحققين ولا يخفى حسنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid is reported to treat the two verbs as synonymous; al-Alusi says this is not sound.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر وجماعة عن مجاهد أنهما بمعنى واحد وليس بذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians either take the verbs as intransitive or as transitive with an omitted object: nothing, or the affairs of the earlier generations, is lost or forgotten.
rows.anchor: والفعلان قيل : منزلان منزلة اللازم وقيل : هما باقيان على تعديهما

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says God does not err about or forget the time of resurrection; al-Alusi notes that this assumes Pharaoh asked about resurrection.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن لا يضل وقت البعث ولا ينساه وكأنه جعل السؤال عن البعث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the promise as God not leaving a disbeliever without retribution or a monotheist without reward, apparently reading the question as one about their ultimate state.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أن المعنى لا يترك من كفر به حتى ينتقم منه ولا يترك من وحده حتى يحازيه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some make the clause an adjective of “book,” with an omitted return pronoun; another parses God as the object, so nothing can make the book lost to him and it omits nothing, like the cited verse.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن الجملة فى موضع الصفة لكتاب والعائد اليه محذوف أي لا يضله ربى ولا ينساه

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة والجحدري وحماد بن سلمة وابن محيصن وعيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: They read “does not lead astray” with a prefixed damma on the yāʾ, from the form meaning to cause something to be lost.
rows.anchor: بضم الياء من اضل واضللت الشئ وضللته قيل بمعنى

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Al-Sikkit distinguishes losing one’s camel from losing one’s way to a mosque or provisions, and generalizes the latter to stationary things whose location cannot be found.
rows.anchor: يقال : اضللت بعيرى إذا ذهب منك وضللت المسجد والزاد إذا لم تعرف موضعهما

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: For this reading, Abu al-Baqa parses “my Lord” either as the object no one can lead away from knowledge or as the subject that does not find the book lost.
rows.anchor: جعل ( ربى ) منصوبا على المفعوليه والمعنى لا يضل أحد ربى عن علمه

rows.speaker: السلمي
rows.claim: Al-Sulami reads both verbs in the passive, with the agent unspecified.
rows.anchor: لا يضل ربى ولا ينسى ببناء الفعليت لما لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi marvels that interpreters abandon the apparent meaning for such strained constructions.
rows.anchor: والعجب كل العجب من العدول عن الظاهر إلى مثل هذه الأقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “my Lord” instead of a pronoun gives pleasure in naming God, adds emphasis, and signals that lordship itself entails freedom from error and forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: واظهار ( ربى ) فى موقع الاضمار للتلذذ بذكره تعالى ولزيادة التقرير

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: One analysis makes God begin speaking after Moses’ words end at “He neither errs nor forgets”; the relative clause then predicates an omitted “He is,” as an explanatory resumption. The Imam says this must be certain.
rows.anchor: كلام موسى عليه السلام قد تم عند قوله تعالى : ( ولاينسى ) فيكون الموصول خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Alternatively, Moses may quote God’s words verbatim, having heard them from him; “for you” rather than “for us” supports this, and the relative may describe “my Lord,” predicate an omitted subject, or be praise in the accusative.
rows.anchor: قد سمعه من الله عز وجل فادرجه بعينه فى كلامه ولذا قال : ( لكم ) دون لنا

rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: A third analysis has Moses speak from himself, then God’s narration shift “I brought forth” into the divine first person; Ibn al-Munir favors this as subtle and closest to straightforward rhetorical shift.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه حسن رقيق الحاشية وهو اقرب الوجوه إلى الالتفات
